item.title: CP2Ksol: A Poisson–Boltzmann Implicit Electrolyte for Constant-Potential and Hybrid-Solvent Simulations in CP2K
item.description:
First-principles simulations of electrified metal/water interfaces need an electrolyte model that describes the charging and polarization of the electrode, a hybrid solvent that joins explicit water to a continuum, and control of the electrode potential. We developed CP2Ksol, an implicit-electrolyte module in CP2K 2026.2, which couples linear and size-modified nonlinear Poisson–Boltzmann electrolytes in isodensity (ISO) and solvent-excluded (SE) cavities with a capacitance-secant constant-potential loop and an atom-following solvent boundary with analytic atomic forces. On the 643 molecules of the FreeSolv database, ISO gives a mean absolute error of 1.93 kcal/mol in hydration free energies. item.title: Does low interfacial resistance guarantee high critical current density? A quantitative review of sodium-metal/NASICON interfaces
item.description:
Solid-state sodium batteries with NASICON-type solid electrolytes (Na3Zr2Si2PO12) are promising for large-scale energy storage. Their development is limited by two challenges at the sodium metal/electrolyte interface. The first is a high interfacial resistance. It arises from the point contacts between the two solids, the poor wetting of NASICON by sodium and a poorly conducting contamination layer formed in air. The second is the penetration of sodium dendrites through the electrolyte, which causes a short circuit and is quantified by the critical current density (CCD). Many strategies, such as surface treatments, interlayers and composite anodes, reduce the interfacial resistance, and a lower resistance is commonly expected to give a higher CCD. This review explains both challenges and summarises these strategies. To examine how far they suppress dendrite penetration, we collected the interfacial resistance and the CCD of 122 cells reported in 49 papers. Among the cells with an interfacial resistance below 30 Ω cm2, 25 of 37 reached a CCD of 1 mA cm−2. Only 10 of 85 cells above this value did, and none of the 27 cells above 300 Ω cm2. Nevertheless, a low interfacial resistance was not sufficient for a high CCD, and several cells reached a high CCD at a moderate resistance. We therefore discuss other factors that limit the CCD, namely void formation during stripping, the electronic conductivity of the electrolyte and defects in its microstructure, and the strategies that address them, such as doping, sintering aids and densification. Finally, perspectives for future research are provided.

Sanjid Shahriar, Supantha Haldar, Muhammad Hasanuzzaman

item.title: Differentiable Coarse-Graining of Phase Equilibria: Learning a Crystallizable Water Model
item.description:
Bottom-up coarse-grained (CG) models are derived from the configurations of a reference model, either by approximating its many-body potential of mean force or by matching its structural correlations, but neither route ensures that the phase equilibria of the reference are reproduced. Trained with differentiable coarse-graining (DiffCG) on the mapped structure and pressure of ice Ih and liquid TIP4P/Ice water, a onebead many-body neural-network model reproduces the densities and radial distribution functions of both phases but predicts a melting temperature 62.5K below that of the reference. We extend DiffCG to phase equilibria by refining this model with an additional objective, the ice–liquid chemical-potential difference at the reference melting temperature, while its structural and pressure objectives are retained. The free-energy anchor is taken from the CG model’s own coexistence point by Gibbs–Helmholtz integration, so that no absolute free energies are required, and changes of the phase free energies are tracked by fixed-cell reweighting with Bennett acceptance ratio offsets.

Zhenghao Wu

item.title: Self-assembly of monovalent anion pillared metal-organic frameworks: linker functionalization matters
item.description:
Monovalent anion pillaring in coordination networks remains a challenging design target because charge balance requires the simultaneous incorporation of additional counteranions within the structure. Here, we show that subtle changes in the substitution pattern of bis(imidazolyl)benzene (bib) linkers can strongly alter the outcome of self-assembly in Cu(II)-based systems with monovalent polyatomic anions. The dimethoxy-substituted ligand 1,1'-(2,5-dimethoxy-1,4-phenylene)bis(1H-imidazole) (bib(OMe)2) reacts with Cu(BF4)2, Cu(ClO4)2 and Cu(NO3)2 to afford three isoreticular monovalent anion-pillared frameworks, {Cu[bib(OMe)2]2X}X (X = BF4−, UdP-30; ClO4−, UdP-31; NO3−, UdP-32), in which Cu-bib(OMe)2 layers are connected by coordinated anions while additional charge-balancing anions are located within the pores. The frameworks crystallize in the monoclinic C2/c space group and differ from previously reported bibCF3-based topological analogues (UdP-10, -11, and -12, containing the same anions) in symmetry, layer geometry, anion arrangement, and pore accessibility. These compounds retain crystallinity upon desolvation and possess accessible microporosity, as evidenced by gas sorption analysis.

Martina Bucci, Matous Kloda, Jan Demel, Marco Taddei, Giulio Bresciani

item.title: Chirality-Dependent Packing and the Visible LMCT Band of Arylethynyl-Substituted Ru(β-diketonate)3 Complexes: A Computational Study
item.description:
Tris(β-diketonato)ruthenium(III) complexes with arylethynyl arms (Ru-Cn) absorb at about 665 nm in solution and in enantiopure thin films but at 733 nm in racemic films. We examine the origin of this chirality dependence computationally for the three model complexes Ru-H, Ru-OMe, and Ru-C1, which have phenylethynyl, 4-methoxyphenylethynyl, and 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenylethynyl arms, respectively, with dispersion-corrected DFT, TD-DFT, and a transition-charge exciton model applied to dimers, chains, and the racemic crystal. For Ru-OMe, homochiral and heterochiral pairs form face-to-face dimers of similar geometry, the homochiral one being 5 kcal mol−1 more stable, and the exciton coupling V is small (|V| ≤ 160 cm−1) in every arrangement, so aggregation shifts the band by less than 10 nm; this result holds with a triple-ζ basis set and with the range-separated functional ωB97X-D3, and Ru-C1 behaves in the same way (homochiral preference 5.2 kcal mol−1, |V| ≤ 101 cm−1). The molecular geometry matters far more, and the geometric parameters differ in the direction of their effect. For Ru-OMe, rotating the aryl rings from the perpendicular orientation into the chelate plane shifts the band to the red (559 → 690 nm), so that the planar conformation reproduces the solution band, and elongating the Ru–O bonds shifts it further to the red (13 nm per 0.01 Å). For both Ru-OMe and Ru-C1, an arm forced to within 4 Å of a neighboring Ru(III) center admixes intermolecular charge transfer and shifts the band to the red as well; the admixture is 20–40% with PBE0, which overestimates it, and at most 16% with ωB97X-D3, and such a contact is not an energy minimum of an isolated pair. The 780–800-nm bands obtained for the arm-over-metal dimers at semiempirical geometries arise mainly from the elongated Ru–O bonds of those geometries. A thin film of racemic Ru-H, measured here, absorbs at 650 nm, 12 nm to the red of its solution band (638 nm), so the parent compound shows no racemate-specific shift and the 733-nm band requires the alkoxy groups. The band of the racemic condensed state is therefore attributed to packing-imposed changes in molecular geometry (Ru–O distances, alkoxy torsion, or an enforced intermolecular contact), not to exciton (J-aggregate) coupling.

Jun Yoshida
